title: A gentle introduction to mathematical simulation in R
text:
1 Preface
This book is a companion to the workshop “A Gentle Introduction to Mathematical Simulation in R” (December 11, 2025).
This book is free and available online. The workshop, however, is paid, as you get the perk of attending a lecture. Still, I would love it if you could donate a dollar or so to any charity for Ukraine!
Some general knowledge of calculus would be helpful, especially differential equations—I included a short introductory section as a small recap. Some basic knowledge of R would also be helpful, notably the use of {ggplot2}. I will give a brief introduction to {gganimation} as well.
I plan to expand this book to cover other modeling topics that were not explored in the workshop, such as incorporating delays into models and SIR models. So please stay tuned.
crumbs: 1  Preface

title: 2  Picasso’s Le Taureau
text:
It is impossible to wholly capture the entirety of complex biological processes. Mathematical models simplify complexity allowing us to glean insights on the biological mechanisms and predict how systems can change if we vary a parameter. It is not uncommon for mathematical modeling to be likened to art. Indeed, Pablo Picasso’s Le Taureau (1945) shows his six litographs that ranges from the realistic, anatomically drawing of the bull to the geometric representation where only the “essence” of the bull remains.
What is a bull? To Picasso, one only needs the stalwart body, the four legs, and the prominent horns. The simplified form captures a large proportion of what bulls look. Similarly, mathematical models aim to generalize, by stripping the complexity and extraneous features, is able to capture the commonality of unique processes.



Ranging from naturalist depiction to stripped down simplification, Picasso’s Le Taureau is a apt metaphor fro mathematical modeling of biological processes.


While there are many different types of mathematical modeling techniques, this book is focused on using ordinary differential equations (ODE’s) and using R to simulate the output.






Books I recommend



For those that are interested in good resources, I highly recommend A Biologist’s Guide to Mathematical Modeling in Ecology and Evolution by Otto and Day. As well as Modeling Life: The Mathematics of Biological Systems by Garfinkel et al. While more focused on disease, I also loved Bjornstad’s Epidemics due to his approach of showing how to code the math.

title: 3  A short recap of derivatives
text:
3.0.1 What is a derivative?
We will be working with ordinary differential equations (ODEs), which we describe as functions that include derivatives. For the purpose of jogging our memory, let’s remind ourselves what a derivative is.
Fundamentally, a derivative describes the rate of change as we are interested in how rapidly a quantity changes. For example, in many ecological models, we are often interested in how the size of the population changes over time. However, because all examples of the derivative use driving as an example, I will opt to do the same. In the figure below, for example, this is the total distance that I drove
We can calculate the average velocity as:
\[
\frac{Point B - Point B}{t_2 - t_1}
\]
In other words, we’re calculating the distance between the points divided by time. And because it’s a straight line, the speed is constant! In other words, the velocity of the car is unchanging. Now what is a derivative, formally is:
\[
\lim_{h\to 0} \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}
\]
Basically, what if we made h, very very small. It’s not going to be 0, but we’re basically thinking about thinking of something much smaller than a second. This makes more sense if our little rat has more realistic driving - for anyone who drives, we know that we never keep constant speed as we brake and accelerate through our journey.
We can plot it out like so:
If we think about our speedometer, we can imagine we have a camera that gives us a snapshot of what the speedometer was at a given time. That’s essentially what a derivative is, telling us at a point in time how the quantity is changing.

title: 4  How does a population grow?
text:
4.1 Hello (silicon) world!
For our first foray into mathematical modeling, let’s start with the model: how does the size of a population change over time? Assume we’re observing a population on an isolated island, \(N\) (which stands for the number of individuals), and we must think of the time scale, \(t\). For fast-growing organisms like bacteria, it would make more sense to observe the population over the span of hours, as they grow rapidly. It would be unwise, however, to use hours for a slow-growing oak tree. For this population of interest, let us assume a daily time step.
The size of the population increases due to new individuals from births or immigration. Likewise, the population decreases due to deaths or from emigration. For simplicity, let’s assume that there are only births and deaths. Mathematically, we can describe the population as: \[
N_{t+1} = N_t + Births - Deaths.
\]
This model assumes discrete time steps where the total population size is the next-time step (\(t+1\)) is just the sum of the current timestep (\(t\)) with the addition and removal of individuals.
crumbs: 4  How does a population grow?

title: 4  How does a population grow?
section: 4.2 The nature of births and deaths
text:
4.2 The nature of births and deaths
Intuitively, we would imagine that the larger a population is, the more births there would be. So it makes sense that the total number of births would depend on the current population size:
\[
Births = b N_t,
\]
where \(b\) is the daily per-capita birth rate, or the number of births per individual in the population per unit-time. For example, if \(b = 0.10\), it would say that each individual should produce 0.10 of an individual. In a population of 100 individuals, 10 new individuals should then be born. This intuition works similarly for deaths: the more individuals there are in a population, the more deaths will occur. Similarly,
\[
Deaths = d N_t,
\]
and \(d\) describes the daily per-capita death rate. All together, our model of population growth looks like this:
\[
\begin{aligned}
N_{t+1} &= N_t + bN_t - dN_t \\
       &= N_t(1 + b - d).
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(b\) and \(d\) are in the same units, we can combine them as \(r = b - d\) with \(r\) being called the geometric rate of increase. What happens if \(r = 0\)? That means \(b = d\), so the number of births and deaths is equal, and the population size does not change. If \(r > 0\), then there are more births than deaths, and the population will increase. Likewise, if \(r < 0\), there are more deaths than births, so the population will decrease. Thus, our final model is:
\[
N_{t+1} = N_t(1 + r),
\]
and we find that as
\[
\frac{N_{t+1}}{N_t} = (1+r),
\]
meaning that \((1+r)\) describes how the population change.






Finite rate of increase



The term \((1+r)\) also has a name called the finite rate of increase. Usually it is replaced by \(\lambda\) and so the above model is usually seen as \(N_{t+1} = \lambda N_t\)
crumbs: 4  How does a population grow?

title: 4  How does a population grow?
text:
4.3 What does the future hold?
The above equation is perfect for when we want to determine the population size at the next time-step. But if we want to start at the initial time point, then it would be as follows:
\[
N_{t} = N_0(1+r)^t,
\]
where \(N_0\) (pronounced N-naught) is the initial population size.






How to generalize



Starting from the initial time (\(t=0\)), the next time step would be:
\[ N_1 = N_0(1+r),
\]
and for \(t=2\) it would be:
\[
\begin{aligned}
N_2 &= N_1(1+r) \\
       &= N_0(1+r)(1 + r) \\
       & = N_0(1+r)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Try doing it for \(t=3\)!
crumbs: 4  How does a population grow?

title: 4  How does a population grow?
text:
4.4 How to code it?
For coding these types of models, we should use functions. As a rule of thumb, the input for these functions should include the parameters, as these can vary. Think of all the things that could be changed in the mathematical model. So let’s look at this function skeleton here, which I call pop_Growth. Generally, simulations of populations involve time (how long you run them for), the parameters of interest, and the initial population size. Here is the skeleton below:

pop_Growth<- function(time, b, d, N0){

}

Now we have the model equation: \(N_t = N_0 (1+r)^t\). What is the output that we want for this function? At each timestep, we should have the population size. While most mathematical modeling books don’t take into account of this Also, generally when we’re running mathematical simulations, you’ll be running the model for multiple combinations of parameters. It’s good to afix the parameter value that you’re looking at as an output. Because of the iterative nature of the above model, it would make sense to use for-loops but the problem is that they are computationally intensive. Thankfully, we can use the inherent capability of R for vectorization in which a function will run on each element of a vector at the same time.






A simple example of vectorization




x = seq(1,5)

print(x * 5)

[1]  5 10 15 20 25





pop_Growth <- function(time, b, d, N0){
    time_step <- seq(1,time)
    r = b - d
    N = N0*(1+r)^(time_step)

    return(data.frame(time_step,N, b,d, N0))
}

You see now that the output is a data.frame that will have the same number of rows equal to time, the population size at the time, as well as the three parameters: birth rate, death rate, and the initial population size. Now let’s try running it:

popGrowth_df <- pop_Growth(time = 25, b = 0.5, d= 0.1, N0 = 100)
head(popGrowth_df, 10)

Congratulations, yon ran your first model!

title: 4  How does a population grow?
text:
4.5 The power of simulation
The power of simulation is that we can explore different parameter combinations. This allows us to examine models across the entire parameter space, which is important because the dynamics can change depending on the parameters we choose. One way to achieve this is by using a handy function called expand.grid, which allows us to generate all possible combinations of parameters.

param_grid <- expand.grid(
  b  = c(0.1, 0.2),
  d  = c(0.05, 0.1),
  N0 = c(50, 100)
)

param_grid

    b    d  N0
1 0.1 0.05  50
2 0.2 0.05  50
3 0.1 0.10  50
4 0.2 0.10  50
5 0.1 0.05 100
6 0.2 0.05 100
7 0.1 0.10 100
8 0.2 0.10 100


You can see that this is all possible combinations of \(b\), \(d\), and \(N_0\) that represent different scenarios. For the first row, for example, this means that the death rate is much higher than the birth rate, and the initial population size is 50. We can compare this to a scenario where the birth rate is higher than the death rate, with the same initial population size.
To run multiple simulations, we use the lapply function:

results <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(
    split(param_grid, seq(nrow(param_grid))),
    function(p) pop_Growth(25, p$b, p$d, p$N0)
  )
)
crumbs: 4  How does a population grow?

title: 4  How does a population grow?
text:
4.6 Plotting it out
Plotting out mathematical simulations can be difficult because of the large number of parameter space that we are looking at. So it is important to have a reason. For example, what if we were interested in only how the initial population changes? Then for direct comparision, we would try to keep the other parameters consistent, so let’s subset the data that we need

results_subset <- subset(results, results$b == 0.10 & results$d == 0.05)

We should have two rows in this data and when we plot it out, we can see that with a greater population size is able to grow faster.

ggplot(results_subset, aes(x = time_step, y = N, group = as.factor(N0), color = as.factor(N0))) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line()+ 
  xlab("Time (days)") + 
  ylab("Abundance") + 
  labs(color = "N0") +
  theme_classic() + 
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 13),
       axis.title = element_text(size = 14))

title: 5  Segway: Discrete to continuous
text:
Previously, the model we were looking at was in discrete time, but the compartmental model we’re examining now is in continuous time. Discrete time makes intuitive sense to us—we tend to think of our daily lives in terms of days. But a continuous model requires thinking in terms of a continuum: a day can be divided into hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds, and even finer intervals. This represents the infinitesimal time scale of continuous time. We like this approach because it is mathematically tractable. Remember our original equation is:
\[
N_{t+1} = N_t(1 + r),
\]
which we can rearrange to be:
\[
N_{t+1} - N_t = r(N_t),
\]
which can be simply explained as the change in the population size between \(t\) and \(t+1\) is \(r(N_t)\). We’re taking daily time steps, but we can also take much smaller time steps. To signify this we use the term \(\Delta t\) :
\[
N_{t + \Delta t} - N_t = \Delta t (r) N_t,
\]
by dividing both sides by \(\Delta t\) which we can write as :
\[
\frac{N_{t + \Delta t} - N_t}{\Delta_t} = r N_{t}
\]
Now what if we get the \(\Delta t\) get really small. It’s approaching 0 (never reaching it), but it’s smaller and smaller. Then we would get
\[
\frac{dN}{dt} = rN(t).
\]
This shows that we can switch between the continuous and discrete form by thinking about reducing the time-scale. As we make the timesteps smaller and smaller, the discrete form converges to the continuous form.
crumbs: 5  Segway: Discrete to continuous

title: 6  The Lotka-Volterra Predator Prey model
text:
6.1 Building the model from the grounds up
The Lotka–Volterra predator–prey model describes the dynamics between predators and their prey. It was formulated independently by the American scientist Alfred Lotka and the Italian scientist Vito Volterra. In Volterra’s case, his son-in-law asked him to explain why predator fish increased in abundance during the war, when fishing of the prey fish was reduced. This led to Volterra’s seminal work in Nature, where he described the predator–prey cycles.
Let’s build the model part-by-part to better understand it.
crumbs: 6  The Lotka-Volterra Predator Prey model

title: 6  The Lotka-Volterra Predator Prey model
text:
6.1.1 A world of only prey
For the Lotka–Volterra model, let us first start with the prey. For the sake of the cover that I spent a lot of time drawing, we can think of the prey animals as hares. Let us describe the hares with \(V\) (some dark humor in that it’s short for “victim”). Now, what is the easiest way to model the population growth? We have already talked about exponential growth, so let’s build the model together:
\[
\frac{dV}{dt} = rV(t),
\]
where \(r\) is the intrinsic growth rate. This model simply states that in the absence of the predator, the rabbits will increase exponentially.


6.1.2 Killed by a predator
Now let us populate our silicon world with a predator, which we describe with \(P\). The prey will then be depleted by being caught by the predator. How do we model this? Well, we have this idea from chemistry called the law of mass action. The rate at which a prey and a predator will meet is determined by their product: \(V(t)P(t)\). But we know that not every meeting will meet with the victim’s death so we have the parameter \(k\) which is often called the kill rate (k):
\[
\frac{dV}{dt} = rV(t) - kV(t)P(t)
\]


6.1.3 The predator must eat
Predators must consume prey to produce more of themselves, so we take the above predation term and add another parameter \(b\). This is called the conversion efficiency, and it tells us the rate at which new individuals are created by the predator catching the prey. \[
\frac{dP}{dt} = bkV(t)P(t)
\]
And then we have a very simple death term here where \(\mu\) is the per-capital mortality rate:
\[
\frac{dP}{dt} = bkV(t)P(t) - \mu P(t)
\]
All together the full model looks like this:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dV}{dt} = rV(t) - kV(t)P(t) \\
\frac{dP}{dt} = bkV(t)P(t) - \mu P(t)
\end{aligned}
\]
crumbs: 6  The Lotka-Volterra Predator Prey model

title: 6  The Lotka-Volterra Predator Prey model
text:
6.2 Checking the units
An important part of checking our mathematical modeling is making sure that the units look right. Let us look at the prey equation and realize that \(\frac{dV}{dt}\) is in the units of \(\frac{individuals}{time}\). When we look at the equation where
\[
\frac{dV}{dt} = rV(t),
\]
we realize that if \(V(t)\) is in units of individuals than \(r\) should have the units of \(\frac{1}{time}\):
\[
\frac{individuals}{time} = \frac{1}{time} \times individuals
\]
Now this is a bit harder, how about the predation term: \(kV(t)P(t)\)? Well let’s look at \(V(t) P(t)\) which would then be \(individuals \times individuals\) or \(individuals^2\). For it to equal the left hand side (\(\frac{individual}{time}\)) then \(k\) has to equal \(\frac{1}{individual \times time}\).






Actually the units are actually canceling each other out



Ok, actually units of \(r\) should really be \(\frac{individuals}{individuals \times time}\) because the intrinsic growth rate actually describes the growth per person per time. However, we can see that because individuals appear in both the numerator and the denominator- it cancels out leaving only \(\frac{1}{time}\)


Therefore, the full units should look this:
\[
\frac{individuals}{time} = \frac{1}{time} \times individuals + \frac{1}{individuals \times time} individuals^2
\]
Try it out with the predator equations!
crumbs: 6  The Lotka-Volterra Predator Prey model

title: 7  Solving the differential equations
text:
7.1 Euler method
For simple ODES, we are able to solve it analytically. For example, for the continuous form of population growth we have:
\[\frac{dN}{dt} = rN(t),
\]
and when we solve it:
\[
N(t) = N_0 e^{rt}.
\]
But the problem is that for many complex ecological models, we are not able to solve them analytically — we can only solve them by numerical simulation! How do we solve differential equations? Remember the earlier method with the discrete model? Well, that only works because we are working in discrete time (each time step is a day). But when we work in continuous time, we are working in the infinitesimal — think of the smallest unit of time you can imagine, and now imagine all the time smaller than that. So we need to think of a method to project forward. I’m going to show you the simplest method, which is called the Euler method.
The Euler method is one way to approximate the solved form of the differential equation. It involves calculating at a predetermined time-step which we call \(h\). And like the discrete population growth model that we worked with, the equation is so:

title: 7  Solving the differential equations
section: 7.2 All this work, but Euler method isn’t great!
text:
7.2 All this work, but Euler method isn’t great!
So generally, the Euler method isn’t very accurate and can be very slow because for it to be accurate, there’s need to be small time-steps and that can be computationally really intensive. So there’s other methods- one that is very common is called Runge-Kutta though the default for the package we’re using uses LSODA. I think you need to be aware of the names.
crumbs: 7  Solving the differential equations

title: 7  Solving the differential equations
text:
7.3 Using deSolve
For a lot of differential equation solving, we use the oldest package called deSolve. This package is very formulaic in what it gives you, you need to give it a function where the output is the derivatives at a time. So generally, we have three inputs: timestep (t), parameters (param), and the variables that will be changing (state).

LV_prey_pred <- function(t, state, param) {
}

and let’s fill it:

LV_prey_pred <- function(t, state, param) {
  with(as.list(c(state, param)), {
    
    dV <- (r * V) - (b * V * P)
    dP <- (a * b * V * P) -  mu * P

    return(list(c(V = dV, P = dP)))
  })
}

So this is the model function ourself, but remember when we’re solving a differential equation what do we need: (1) how long to run the model, (2) what are the parameter values and (3) what is the initial abundance? For time, how about we look at 5 years?

times <- 1:(365 * 5) # 5 years

And for parameters, we need to think about the rates and that everything would be in time. The model itself is agnostic to time, nothing about the model formulation would change if we want to work in terms of a month or a year, only the rates which we would have to convert.

param <- c(r= 1, b = 0.02, a = 0.5, mu = 0.2)

and the states are:

states <- c(V = 1,P = 2)


lv_results <- ode(y = states, times = times, func = LV_prey_pred, parms = param)

head(lv_results, 10)

      time            V          P
 [1,]    1   1.00000000   2.000000
 [2,]    2   2.62085998   1.665226
 [3,]    3   6.90863176   1.425013
 [4,]    4  18.27762397   1.311295
 [5,]    5  48.35844067   1.462670
 [6,]    6 126.56372216   2.703989
 [7,]    7 300.08735342  17.260930
 [8,]    8 111.03698385 231.692474
 [9,]    9   1.71795304 248.082152
[10,]   10   0.05126931 204.020707


See you can see the data.frame that includes the time as well as the total abundnace of the prey and predator.






The default solver in deSolve is called LSODA



If you don’t define a method in deSolve, it goes to LSODA which switches between two solvers! I think it’s worth knowing what the names are BUT it can be a fun read to figure out how they do the algorithim.

title: 8  Visualizing dynamics
text:
8.1 Using ggplot to make the plots
Starting from our previous model, here we’re going to use graphs to understand our model a bit better. What does this graph look like? Let’s use ggplot2 (though base plot also works!) to graph it. Now remember that our data.frame should be reshaped so that it’s a bit easier to work with:
lv_results_melt <- melt(lv_results, id.vars = 'time')
So let’s plot it out:
ggplot(lv_results_melt, aes(x = time, y = value, color = variable, group = variable)) + 
    geom_line() +
     theme_classic() +
     xlab("Time (Day)") + 
     ylab("Abundance") +
    theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 12))
So what does that tell us, it tells us that we’re thinking abut things in a cycle. Now let me show you animations. Making animations without ggplot used to be a clunky back then, but I find them so easy (just an additional coding line) that it’s not a gimmick to make.
animation <- ggplot(lv_results_melt, aes(x = time, y = value, color = variable)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_classic() +
  xlab("Time (Day)") +
  ylab("Abundance") +
  transition_reveal(time) +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 12))

animate(animation, duration = 15)
So we can see that as the prey population increases, the population of the predator will also increase due to the greater resources. However, as the population of the predator increases, they will predate more of the prey, and the prey decreases and thus the predator decrease well. This leads to the cycles.
